The study design (RCT) and intervention type (systemic) fully match the review's selection criteria: randomised controlled trials assessing topical or systemic interventions for alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, and alopecia universalis.

This is a randomized, placebo-controlled trial evaluating oral prednisolone (a systemic intervention) for extensive alopecia areata. It directly addresses the review's objective and meets the selection criteria of RCTs that evaluate systemic interventions for alopecia areata.

This is a multicenter, prospective, randomized, investigator-blinded trial comparing two topical corticosteroid formulations (betamethasone valerate foam vs betamethasone dipropionate lotion) for mild-to-moderate alopecia areata. It meets the selection criteria as a randomized controlled trial evaluating the effectiveness of a topical intervention for alopecia areata. The outcome (hair regrowth) directly addresses treatment efficacy. Although the population is limited to mild-to-moderate AA, the protocol encompasses all alopecia areata, totalis, and universalis trials; thus, inclusion is appropriate.

This study is a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial with random allocation to either topical minoxidil or placebo, clearly an RCT. It evaluates a topical intervention (3% minoxidil) for extensive alopecia areata, including alopecia totalis and universalis, matching the population and intervention criteria. The outcomes assess hair growth. Therefore it meets the selection criteria for this systematic review.

This is a double-blind, placebo-controlled randomised controlled trial evaluating a topical intervention (3% minoxidil) for extensive alopecia areata. The study directly assesses the effectiveness of a topical treatment for alopecia areata, matching the review's population, intervention, and study design criteria. Since it is a RCT testing a topical therapy for the condition of interest, it clearly meets the selection criteria.
This is an RCT testing topical DPCP and minoxidil for alopecia areata, fulfilling all criteria: population (alopecia areata), intervention (topical), and study design (RCT).

This is a randomised controlled trial that randomly assigned patients with alopecia totalis/universalis to topical cyclosporine (topical intervention), PUVA (systemic phototherapy), and intravenous thymopentin (systemic immunotherapy). The study evaluates both topical and systemic interventions for alopecia areata variants, meeting the population (alopecia totalis/universalis) and intervention types specified in the selection criteria. The study design is an RCT, fitting the required study design. Although the participants were non-responders to sensitising therapy, this is a subpopulation of the target condition, and the trial still addresses effectiveness of interventions for alopecia areata. Therefore, it should be included.

The study is not a randomised controlled trial. It is a small case series in six patients with within-subject comparisons of different concentrations of ALA lotion, and does not employ randomization or a control group. The selection criteria require RCTs evaluating interventions for alopecia areata.
Randomized controlled trial evaluating a topical intervention (cyclosporin A) for alopecia areata, matching the review's population, intervention, and study design criteria.

This is a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial evaluating the systemic intervention imipramine for alopecia areata. Although the abstract does not explicitly state 'randomized', double-blind, placebo-controlled designs are inherently RCTs, and the selection criteria require randomised controlled trials. The study directly addresses a systemic intervention for alopecia areata, matching the population, intervention, and outcome components. Therefore, it meets the inclusion criteria. I include conservatively due to the implied randomisation.

This is a randomized controlled trial (patients were randomly assigned to three groups) evaluating a topical intervention (topical immunotherapy with squaric acid dibutylester) and a systemic intervention (lymphoblastoid interferon alpha intramuscular), as well as their combination, for alopecia areata (chronic severe/recalcitrant). The study directly assesses the effectiveness of both topical and systemic treatments, matching the review's eligibility criteria.

=== SCREENING TASK: Study 13 ===

SELECTION CRITERIA:
Randomised controlled trials that evaluated the effectiveness of both topical and systemic interventions for alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, and alopecia universalis.

STUDY TITLE:
Efficacy and safety of a new clobetasol propionate 0.05% foam in Alopecia areata: A randomised, double-blind placebo controlled trial. Abstract P08.17

STUDY ABSTRACT:
Background  Clinical efficacy of topical corticosteroids in alopecia areata (AA) is still controversial. Positive clinical results have been obtained using ointments with occlusive dressing but this approach has a low patient compliance. Recently, a new topical formulation (thermophobic foam: Versafoam®) of clobetasol propionate 0.05% has been introduced on the market (Olux®, Mipharm, Milan, Italy) (CF). This formulation is easy to apply. After application to the skin the foam quickly evaporates without residues and it has a good patient compliance. In vitro studies have also shown that this formulation enhances the delivery of the active compound through the skin. Aim  To evaluate the efficacy, safety and tolerability of CF in the treatment of moderate to severe AA. Subjects and methods  Thirty‐four patients with moderate to severe AA (eight men, mean age 40 ± 13 years) were enrolled in a randomized, double‐blind, right‐to‐left, placebo‐controlled, 24‐week trial. Alopecia grading score (AGS) was calculated at baseline and after 12 and 24 weeks of treatment using a 0–5 score (0 = no alopecia; 5 = alopecia totalis). Clobetasol foam and the corresponding placebo foam (PF) were applied twice a day for 5 days/week for 12 weeks (phase 1) using an intrapatient design (right vs. left). From weeks 13 to 24 each enrolled patient continued only with the treatment (both on the right and left site) that was judged to have a greater efficacy than that on the contralateral side (phase 2). The primary outcome of the trial, evaluated on an intention‐to‐treat basis, was the hair regrowth rate, which was evaluated using a semiquantitative score (RGS) (from 0: no regrowth, to 4: regrowth of  75%). Results  At baseline the AGS was 4.1 (range: 2–5). Nine (26%) patients prematurely concluded the trial. At the end of phase 1, a greater hair regrowth was observed in 89% of the head sites treated with CF vs. 11% in the sites treated with PF. The RGS was 1.2 ± 1.6 in the CF‐treated sites and 0.4 ± 0.8 in the PF‐treated sites (P = 0.001). A RGS of  2 (hair regrowth of more than 25%) was observed in 42% CF‐treated sites and in 13% of PF‐treated sites (P = 0.027). In seven subjects (20%) a RGS of 3 to 4 (hair regrowth of  50%) was observed in CF‐treated sites. In three subjects (9%) a RGS of 4 (hair regrowth of  75%) was observed in CF‐treated sites. In one patient only, in a PF‐treated region, a RGS of 3 was observed. The AS was reduced to 3.8 by CF treatment at the end of phase 1 and to 3.3 at the end of phase 2 (P = 0.01). From weeks 12 to 24 the treatment with CF induced a further increase in the RGS (from 1.2 to 1.5 ± 1.4). Forty‐seven per cent of CF‐treated patients had a RGS of  2 at the end of the trial. A total of eight patients (25%) at the end of the treatment with CF showed a RGS of  3. Folliculitis occurred in two patients. No significant modifications in cortisol and ACTH blood levels were observed during the trial. Conclusion  This new formulation of clobetasol propionate foam is an effective, safe and well‐tolerated topical treatment for AA. This formulation has a good cosmetic acceptance and patient compliance profile.Wiley Online Library

INSTRUCTIONS: Based on the selection criteria above, decide whether this study should be INCLUDED or EXCLUDED. Provide a brief rationale tied to specific criteria.

The study is a randomized controlled trial (explicitly stated) evaluating systemic prednisone (a systemic intervention) and topical minoxidil (a topical intervention) for the treatment of alopecia areata, and it includes patients with alopecia totalis and universalis. This fits all PICO elements: population (alopecia areata, totalis, universalis), intervention (both systemic and topical), comparison (prednisone alone vs prednisone + minoxidil, and vehicle control), and outcome (hair regrowth). The study directly meets the review\'s selection criteria for RCTs assessing effectiveness of both topical and systemic interventions for alopecia areata spectrum disorders.

The study describes a double-blind, placebo-controlled trial of topical minoxidil in patients with extensive alopecia areata (25–100% scalp involvement). This design is consistent with a randomized controlled trial, meeting the review's criteria for RCTs evaluating topical interventions for alopecia areata. The study population includes alopecia areata and possibly totalis/universalis. When in doubt, we include.

The study is a controlled trial comparing topical therapies (squaric acid dibutylester, diphencyprone, minoxidil) against placebo in patients with patchy alopecia areata, which aligns with the population and intervention criteria. Although the abstract does not explicitly state randomization, it is described as a controlled trial, and in a conservative screening approach, it is reasonable to infer it could be an RCT. Therefore, it should be included to allow full-text review to confirm randomization and other eligibility details.

This is a cross-sectional survey evaluating illness perceptions among patients with alopecia areata. It is not a randomized controlled trial and does not evaluate any topical or systemic intervention for alopecia areata. Therefore, it does not meet the fundamental study design criterion of being an RCT that evaluates an intervention for alopecia areata.

The study is a methodological commentary discussing when randomized trials are unnecessary based on large treatment effects, using historical examples. It is not a randomized controlled trial, nor does it evaluate any topical or systemic intervention for alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, or alopecia universalis. The population, intervention, and outcome are entirely unrelated to the review's criteria. Therefore, it clearly does not meet the inclusion criteria.

This is a randomized, double-blind, controlled trial (RCT) that investigated the efficacy of aromatherapy (a topical intervention) in patients with alopecia areata. The study compared daily scalp massage with essential oils (thyme, rosemary, lavender, cedarwood in carrier oils) versus carrier oils alone. Outcome measures included photographic assessment of hair regrowth by blinded dermatologists. The design, population, intervention, comparator, and outcome are all consistent with the review's inclusion criteria for RCTs evaluating topical interventions for alopecia areata. Therefore, it meets the protocol requirements.

The study appears to be a narrative review or update on alopecia areata, not a randomized controlled trial. The abstract does not describe any randomized comparison, control group, or prospective intervention evaluation; it merely summarizes current understanding of pathogenesis and mentions that certain treatments have been successful in the majority of patients. There is no indication that the study itself is an RCT, nor does it report any results from an RCT. Therefore it does not meet the selection criteria, which require randomised controlled trials evaluating interventions for AA/totalis/universalis.

This is a retrospective descriptive study of incidence and natural history, not an RCT evaluating interventions for alopecia areata. It clearly does not meet the protocol's selection criteria requiring randomised controlled trials of topical or systemic interventions.

The study examines prognostic factors in 139 patients treated with diphenylcyclopropenone. It is not described as a randomized controlled trial; no mention of random allocation or a comparison group is present. The objective is to identify predictors of prognosis, not to evaluate the effectiveness of an intervention against a control. Thus, it does not meet the inclusion criterion of being a randomized controlled trial evaluating interventions for alopecia areata.

The study is a controlled trial that evaluates both a topical intervention (diphencyprone, a contact sensitizer applied to the scalp) and a systemic intervention (oral inosine pranobex) for alopecia totalis, which falls under the scope of alopecia areata. It includes a comparison of three groups: inosine pranobex alone, diphencyprone alone, and the combination. Although the abstract does not explicitly state that allocation was randomised, it describes dividing subjects into three groups matched for age and sex, which is consistent with a controlled trial design. Given the conservative screening principle (when in doubt, include), this study should proceed to full-text review to confirm randomisation.

This is a review article focusing on the genetic basis of alopecia areata and future research into genetic susceptibility. It is not a randomized controlled trial and does not evaluate the effectiveness of any topical or systemic intervention for alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, or alopecia universalis. Therefore it clearly does not meet the review's inclusion criteria of study design (RCT) or intervention evaluation.

This study is a methodological article about assessing the quality of controlled clinical trials, not a randomized controlled trial evaluating any topical or systemic intervention for alopecia areata. It discusses concepts of internal and external validity in trials in general. It clearly does not meet the selection criteria, which require an RCT on interventions for alopecia areata, alopecia totalis, or alopecia universalis.
